\[
4g(f(\sin(2\pi x)))=4\bigl||\,\bigl||\,\lvert\sin(2\pi x)\rvert- \tfrac12\bigl|-\tfrac14\bigl| .

If \(z\in[0,1]\) set

\[
H(z)\equiv 4\bigl||\,\bigl||\,z- \tfrac12\bigl|-\tfrac14\bigl| .

For the output of \(H\) we analyze the two regions

\[
\text{(i)}\; |z-1/2|\le \tfrac14 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
  H(z)=1-4|z-1/2|,
\]

\[
\text{(ii)}\; |z-1/2|\ge \tfrac14 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
  H(z)=4|z-1/2|-1 .
\]

### 2.  Mapping \(x\mapsto y\)

Let  

\[
z=\lvert\sin(2\pi x)\rvert .
\]

The function \(z\) vanishes at \(x=\tfrac12\) and equals \(1\) at \(x=0,1\); it is
symmetric on \([0,1]\) and periodic with period \(1\).

With \(y=4g(f(\sin(2\pi x)))=H(z)\) the “y–graph’’ is therefore

\[
y(x)=
\begin{cases}
1-4|z-1/2| , & z\in[0.25,0.75],\\[4pt]
4|z-1/2|-1 , & z\in[0,0.25]\cup[0.75,1].
\end{cases}
\]

The function has a maximum value \(y=1\) when
\(z=0\) or \(z=1\) (i.e. \(x=0,\,\tfrac12,\,1\)), and \(y=0\) when
\(\lvert z-1/2\rvert=0.25\) (i.e. \(z=0.25,0.75\)).

### 4.  Intersection points

The two equations must hold simultaneously, i.e.

\[
y=4g(f(\sin(2\pi x)))\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x=4g(f(\cos(3\pi y))).
\]

We find that \(x=1\) and \(y=1\) satisfy both equations, because
\(z=1\) and \(w=1\) lead to \(g(f)=\tfrac14\) which gives \(4g(f)=1\).

Suppose \((x,y)\) is any other intersection.

* If \(y=1\) then \(x=4g(f(\cos(3\pi y)))=1\); hence \(x=1\)

  contradicting the requirement that \(x=1\).
* If \(y=0\) we obtain \(x=1\); but \(y=0\) for \(x=\tfrac12\) or

* If \(0<y<1\) then \(x\) is strictly less than \(1\) (since the
